questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: One of the most important aspects was they offer interesting and challenging courses, and that the university has a good reputation within my field of study. It was also important to me that the exams were held no later than end of January. I also chose UvA because Amsterdam is known to be a very multi-cultural city, and the Netherlands are considered a safe country.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The workload was higher than I anticipated based on the experiences that friends of mine had in other universities and countries. That is the main reason why I did not rate the experience 10/10.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Before and upon arrival UvA send out several newsletters containing relevant information about my stay.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an introduction day for exchange students at the Economics and Business department the week before classes strated, where we received a lot of information and went on a campus tour.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I was lucky to win the housing lottery, and receive cheap accommodation (a shared dorm) right next to campus. Many other exchange students received housing in the outskirts of the city, and had to bike 30-50 minutes to get to campus. 
The university can offer housing to approximately half of the exchange students, and the housing is distributed randomly using a lottery. If you do not receive housing through the university, it can be very hard and very expensive to find something on your own due to the housing crisis in Amsterdam.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Housing can be extremely expensive in Amsterdam (even worse than Copenhagen), and you may have to live 30-50 minutes bicycle distance from capmus. Other than that it is generally considered a safe city.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
As a master's students the registration process was different from the bachelor's students'. We received an email with a link to a registration form containing all the courses that the host university allowed us to apply for. It was easy to fill in, but you do not receive any e-mail confirmation after the form is filled in. Also, you have to log on to
sis.uva.nl
to find out if you were accepted into the courses that you applied for, as they will not send you an e-mail or anything when your course registration is accepted.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can write an email or call the Economics and Business Exchange office. They usually answer to emails within 3 days.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was accepted into all 6 classes that I applied for. However, before I knew which courses UvA would allow me to take, I had planned on applying for some different courses. I was able to apply for 4 out of 6 courses that I had planned to apply for, and I had to choose 2 new courses from the list of courses available to me.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Send them an email before course registration, to find out exactly which courses you are eligible to apply for according to the host university.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took 1 BA course and 5 MA courses. The BA course was easy enough (as expected). One of the MA courses (Microeconomics and Game Theory) was way harder than I had expected, as it sounded easy according to the course discription, but the work load was very high and the way they grade the exams is different from back home (minor calculus mistakes can severely pull down your grade).
For me, the rest of the MA courses were not too hard.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They expected you to study more independently than at KU. At KU we would have tutorial classes were the TA goes through all problem sets, but at UvA the tutorials were mostly like Q&A sessions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Management Accounting 1 for Business (BA couse)
Managerial Economics (MA course)
Microeconomics and Game Theory (MA course)
Behavioural Economics (MA course)
Advanced Industrial Organisations (MA course)
Advanced Game Theory (MA course)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Managerial Economics: easy course, the professor is very nice.
Behavioural Economics: it was fun, a lot to read, and the tutorial classes consisted of the students presenting a paper, so it was nice to do something different for once.
Advanced Industrial Organisations: same professor as Managerial Economics. The professor said it was one of the most difficult courses in their Master's program (because of the "difficult" math), but I do not think it was that difficult - there are way harder courses back home.
Advanced Game Theory: fun if you like game theory, the professor is a bit absent-minded, the work load is not too bad, and the exam is fair.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The only thing I can think of is that we had to buy all the equipment for the kitchen, as the dorm building throws everything out after you move out. This includes pots, pans, electric kettle, plates, cutlery, glasses. This ended up costing around 250 EUR (I shared this cost with my roommate)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Dairy products and coffee in cafes were a bit cheaper. 
I feel like meat was more expensive, but not a lot.
Restaurants and other groceries were more or less the same as in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
USC (the university sports college) offers almost any sport you can think of (including a cheap fitness membership), but some sports are very popular so you have to be quick if you want a spot.
CREA offers different dance and music classes and almost all thinkable creative courses (ceramics, painting, etc.). Also these classes are quickly filled up, so you have to be quick to get a spot.
ESN Amsterdam host several parties, movie nights, trips abroad and trips to other Dutch cities, and other social events - some are free and some have a fee.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Anything at CREA. Dutch Movie Night hosted by ESN Amsterdam.
And I highly recommend participating in the ESN Introduction Program in the end of August -  it is intense, but also a great way of meeting other exchange students.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Visit Belgium, or visit other Dutch cities like Rotterdam, Haarlem, Utrecht, Den Haag or Zandvoort (Den Haag and Zandvoort have nice beaches!). If the weather is good, you can even bike to some nearby towns.
Get yourself a Museumcard! It is 65 EUR, but lasts one year, 
and you can visit many of the biggest and most famous museums "for free" with this card (400+ museums in the Netherlands, and around 50 museums in Amsterdam)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy enough as a Dane. The culture is not that different. They are straightforward people, it feels safe, and the way you interact with the professors is very informal, just like at home.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: In the break you should just talk to the person sitting next to you in class. If you are single, go on dates. Join a sport or creative class at CREA.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Especially in the service sector (restaurants, cafes, etc.) the staff can seem rude, but that is just because they are VERY straightforward and have this no-bullshit attitude.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How multi-cultural the city is, and how chill and informal people are.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be open to new people and cultures, and try to meet new people that are not only Danes!
Get yourself a bicycle as soon as you arrive! (Swapfiets is very easy to use)
Be spontaneous and say yes to plans and invitations, and remember to have fun, and don't worry too much about the studies!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Can't think of anything atm.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Making new friends from all over the world (from Australia to Canada, and Botswana to Finland).
And just being able to be more spontaneous than I usually would be back home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Balancing studies with all the things I wanted to see and do while I was there. It is like you want to be a tourist and do all the fun stuff, but you are also a local and have to study and pass your classes.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
